v.q: What is a transitive dependency?
o: A library that one of your direct dependencies needs, which comes along automatically
A library declared twice in the same pom with two different versions
A library that is only used by the test classes of your project
A library that the build downloads but never puts on a classpath
v.w: You did not declare it, but it is on the classpath because a library you did declare depends on it.

v.q: A fat jar contains log4j-core, yet the pom never mentions it. What is the most likely reason?
o: It arrived as a transitive dependency of another library
The compiler plugin adds it to every project by default
The jar plugin copies it from the local repository
The JVM supplies it at run time for all applications
v.w: Most libraries in a service are transitive. The dependency tree shows which direct dependency brought it.

v.q: Which command shows every path to a library, including versions that lost a conflict, in Maven?
o: mvn dependency:tree -Dverbose
mvn help:effective-pom
mvn versions:display-plugin-updates
mvn compile -X
v.w: dependency:tree with -Dverbose lists the omitted versions and why they were omitted.

v.q: Which Gradle command explains why a version of a library was chosen?
o: ./gradlew dependencyInsight --dependency <name>
./gradlew tasks --all
./gradlew build --scan-off
./gradlew wrapper --gradle-version
v.w: dependencyInsight shows the selected version and the paths and rules that led to it.

v.q: What does importing a BOM do?
o: It supplies tested versions, so dependencies can be declared without a version
It downloads every library listed in it into the project
It removes all transitive dependencies from the build
It signs each dependency with a trusted key
v.w: A BOM only manages versions. A library is on the classpath only when you declare it.

v.q: Why do Spring Boot starters usually have no version in the pom?
o: The Boot parent or BOM manages the versions
Maven always picks the latest release when no version is given
Starters are built into the JDK
The version is read from the settings.xml of each developer
v.w: spring-boot-dependencies is a BOM, imported by the Boot parent, so versions come from it.

v.q: Two libraries need different versions of Jackson at the same depth. Which does Maven choose?
o: The one declared first in the pom
The highest version number
The lowest version number
The one with the smaller jar file
v.w: Maven chooses the nearest, and on a tie the first declaration. It does not choose the newest.

v.q: How do you make a version win in Maven regardless of what the libraries want?
o: Declare it directly or manage it in dependencyManagement
Rename the library in the local repository
Delete the other version from ~/.m2
Run the build with the -o flag
v.w: A direct declaration is nearest, and dependencyManagement fixes the version for the whole tree.

v.q: Two paths request Jackson 2.12 and 2.15 in Gradle. Which version does it select by default?
o: 2.15, the highest requested
2.12, the first one found
Neither, the build always fails
Whichever is smaller on disk
v.w: Gradle picks the highest requested version unless a constraint or strict version says otherwise.

v.q: How can a Gradle build fail instead of silently choosing a version?
o: resolutionStrategy.failOnVersionConflict()
org.gradle.parallel=true
tasks.register("fail")
Using the wrapper
v.w: failOnVersionConflict turns a disagreement in the tree into a build failure.

v.q: After adding a library the service throws NoSuchMethodError. What is the usual cause?
o: An older version of a library won the conflict than the caller was built for
The JVM is too new for the bytecode
A test class was packaged into the jar
The pom has a duplicate plugin entry
v.w: The class loaded at run time lacks a method the calling library expects, so the wrong version won.

v.q: Why does a version conflict often pass the build and fail later?
o: Both jars compile, and the missing method is only hit at run time
Maven does not read transitive dependencies during compile
Gradle hides compile errors in the build cache
The compiler ignores classes from a repository
v.w: Compilation succeeds against whichever version is on the classpath, and the failure appears on the code path that needs the other one.

v.q: What does the Maven Enforcer dependencyConvergence rule do?
o: Fails the build when the tree has different versions of one library
Downloads the newest version of every library
Removes unused libraries from the pom
Signs the artifacts before upload
v.w: It makes disagreement explicit so the team decides the version instead of the tool guessing.

v.q: Which Enforcer rule keeps an unwanted library such as commons-logging out of the build?
o: bannedDependencies
requireJavaVersion
requireReleaseDeps
dependencyConvergence
v.w: bannedDependencies fails the build if a listed library appears anywhere in the tree.

v.q: Why are SNAPSHOT versions a problem for a release build?
o: Their content can change under the same version
They cannot be downloaded from Nexus
They are always larger than release jars
They are only valid for Gradle
v.w: A snapshot is replaced in place, so you cannot say exactly what code shipped.

v.q: Which of these makes a build least reproducible?
o: A version range such as [1.0,2.0) or 1.+
A fixed version in dependencyManagement
A pinned plugin version
A checked-in Gradle wrapper
v.w: A range resolves to whatever has been published most recently, so the same commit can build differently.

v.q: What does a Gradle lock file record?
o: The exact resolved version of every library in the tree
Only the versions of the direct dependencies
The time of the last build
The list of tasks that ran
v.w: Locking records the full resolved graph, so the same commit resolves the same libraries.

v.q: What does Gradle dependency verification add?
o: A checksum check of every downloaded artifact
Faster downloads from the build cache
A second copy of the dependency tree
Automatic upgrades to the latest version
v.w: verification-metadata.xml stores a SHA-256 (and optional key) per artifact, and the build fails if the bytes differ.

v.q: What is a CVE?
o: A public identifier for one known vulnerability
A score from 0 to 10 for a project's code quality
A build plugin that scans containers
A licence type for open source
v.w: For example CVE-2021-44228. The score that rates its severity is the CVSS.

v.q: A CVE has a CVSS score of 9.8. How is it classed?
o: Critical
Low
Informational
Not exploitable
v.w: A score from 9.0 to 10.0 is critical. Many gates fail the build at 7 or above.

v.q: What does a dependency scan in CI compare?
o: The resolved dependency tree against a database of known vulnerabilities
The source code against a style guide
The test coverage against the last build
The jar size against a limit
v.w: Tools such as OWASP Dependency-Check match names and versions in the tree with CVE data.

v.q: A scan reports a false positive. What is the right way to handle it?
o: Add a reviewed suppression with a reason and an expiry date
Lower the failing threshold to 10
Delete the scan plugin from the pom
Disable the scan for the whole module
v.w: A narrow, documented, time-limited suppression keeps the gate meaningful.

v.q: What made Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228) so hard to deal with in large organisations?
o: The library was often a transitive dependency inside jars nobody had listed
It only affected applications written in Kotlin
It could only be fixed by changing the JVM version
It was found in the Maven build itself
v.w: The hard part was finding where log4j-core was, not applying the fix.

v.q: How can you fix a vulnerable library that you only use transitively?
o: Force a fixed version with a constraint or dependencyManagement entry
Wait for the library to be removed from Maven Central
Rename the package in your own source code
Add the vulnerable version as a runtime dependency
v.w: Managing the version in your own build overrides what the transitive chain asks for.

v.q: What is an SBOM?
o: A machine-readable list of every component in a build with versions and hashes
A signed archive of the source code
A report of failed tests
A configuration file for the repository manager
v.w: CycloneDX and SPDX are common formats. It answers whether a release contains a vulnerable component.

v.q: When a new CVE is announced, how does an SBOM help?
o: You search the stored SBOMs to find affected services without opening jars
It automatically upgrades the library everywhere
It blocks the build for all teams
It removes the vulnerable class from running JVMs
v.w: It turns the question into a query over inventory data.

v.q: What does a repository manager such as Nexus do for a build?
o: Proxies and caches public libraries, hosts internal ones and gives one URL
Compiles the code on behalf of the developer
Runs the unit tests in parallel
Replaces the version control server
v.w: Builds depend on one trusted source, which is fast, auditable and can block bad components.

v.q: Why must a released version in a hosted repository be immutable?
o: So the same version always means the same bytes
Because Maven cannot read a changed file
To save disk space on the server
Because Gradle does not support updates
v.w: If a release can be overwritten, you cannot know what a given version contains.

v.q: What is dependency confusion?
o: A public package with an internal name and a higher version replaces the internal one
Two modules in the same build using the same artifactId
A library with a licence that conflicts with another
A build that fails because of a missing parent pom
v.w: The build asks several repositories for one name and takes the highest version, which the attacker controls.

v.q: Which defence stops a public repository from serving your internal group id?
o: A routing rule that blocks that group id on the public proxy
Using a longer version number
Running the build offline once a week
Adding a sleep to the pipeline
v.w: Routing rules make internal names resolvable only from the hosted repository.
